docs.title: ROS 2 Blueprint Studio
docs.text: A visual editor for ROS 2 that produces real ROS 2 code. Draw nodes and wires, and Studio generates the package (C++ and Python sources, CMakeLists.txt, package.xml, launch files, Dockerfile), builds it with colcon and runs it in Docker. The same project builds and runs on a robot over SSH. No local ROS 2 installation needed: it works on Windows and Linux.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
• New to ROS 2, or to Studio? The tutorials follow the official ROS 2 Humble tutorials in Studio, chapter by chapter, starting from creating a package.
  • Installing: see Install in the repository (Docker is the only requirement besides Studio itself).
  • Before a real project: read the known limitations.

docs.title: What Studio does
docs.text:
Graph → real package every node is a file you own; CMakeLists.txt and package.xml are generated, with a USER block for your own CMake Topics and services publishers, subscribers, service servers and clients in Python and C++; wires keep names in step Run in Docker save, build, launch and per-node logs in one click; the local session is isolated from your network Live parameters sliders for declared ranges, the node's own refusals shown, values saved for the next run Managed nodes Freeze / Unfreeze lifecycle nodes, locally or on the robot Robot over SSH sync only what changed, detect conflicts, build with colcon on the robot, cancel cleanly Deploy groups one launch file per group and a docker-compose.yml to split a graph between machines

Caution

Studio is not a safety system. On a real robot keep its own emergency stop at hand.

docs.title: Known limitations (0.6.0)
docs.text: ROS 2 Blueprint Studio is alpha software. This page lists what is known to be missing or different from what you might expect, so you do not have to find out the hard way.

docs.title: Platforms and runtime
docs.text:
• Docker is required. Nodes are built and run inside a container; there is no native-ROS mode.
  • ROS 2 Humble only. The distribution is fixed in the generated build and rosdep steps.
  • Windows and Linux are the supported platforms. macOS has not been tested; display forwarding for classic X11/RViz mode is not set up there. Foxglove mode needs no X server.
  • Most automated tests fake Docker. The parameter bridge, lifecycle, launch with params.yaml and the service nodes are also tested against a real ROS 2 Humble container when the image is present; the rest of the container behaviour is covered by fakes and manual runs.
  • The packed EXE reads nothing from the source tree: build it with the --add-data list from the README, or translations and the parameter bridge are missing. Its user palettes live in ~/.ros_blueprint_studio/user_palettes.

docs.title: Build and run speed
docs.text:
• The first Run of a project creates a container and installs dependencies (apt + rosdep): expect roughly 30–60 seconds. Later Runs reuse the stopped container, skip the dependency step while package.xml and the extra apt list are unchanged, and take about 1 s (Python) to a few seconds (C++).
  • The reused container keeps build/ and install/. Results of nodes you deleted can linger there. There is no "recreate session" button yet; the container is recreated automatically when the ROS network settings change (domain, DDS, Real robot).
  • Each Run appends phase timings to <project>/.blueprint/timings.jsonl.

docs.title: Graph and generated code
docs.text:
• Names connect nodes, wires keep them in step. ROS matches topic and service names; the generated code takes them from the node fields. Connecting a wire copies the name (publisher → subscriber, server → client) and Save warns about wired nodes whose names differ. Once you edit a node's code, the code decides. Exec-trigger ports (ExecIn/ExecOut) are not generated yet.
  • C++ node names come from the file. The generated launch file names each C++ node after its file (the title on the canvas); the Name field is used by Python nodes only.
  • Run starts project_launch.py only. Your own launch files in src/launch are kept, but you start them from a terminal in the session container.
  • Dependencies are detected from #include lines against a built-in registry. An include that is not in the registry is reported as a warning, not installed.
  • Editing code in two places at once. If a node's code is changed both in Studio and in the file on disk between two saves, the file wins and a warning is written to the log.
  • Python nodes are started as plain scripts by the generated launch file; C++ nodes are built with colcon.

docs.title: Single canvas (default in 0.6.0)
docs.text:
• One canvas holds Python and C++ nodes together. The project is saved in the v4 state format. Studio 0.5.x cannot open it; on the first v4 write the old state is kept as .blueprint/state.v3.6.yaml.bak.
  • The old two-tab mode is still available (checkbox in the launcher, applies on next start). Opening a v4 project in that mode splits nodes by language; wires between a Python and a C++ node are lost.

docs.title: Robots and remote hosts
docs.text:
• The core only provides a generic SSH connection (host, user, password). Vendor-specific robot integrations are not part of the core and are expected as extensions.
  • A local Run is isolated from the network (ROS_LOCALHOST_ONLY=1); turn on Real robot to reach robots on the network. Deploy groups started with docker-compose.yml are not isolated: they are meant to talk across machines.
  • Real-robot networking (DDS settings, multi-host discovery) is configurable per deploy group but has not been validated against physical hardware by the project.
  • A DDS QoS profile set on the Containers tab is mounted for docker-compose services, not for the local Run.
  • The service nodes use example_interfaces, which is in the default image (osrf/ros:humble-desktop) but not in the smaller ros:humble-ros-core/ros-base images.

docs.title: Interface
docs.text:
• UI languages: English and Russian. Switching the language updates the toolbar immediately; other panels pick it up after a restart.
  • Deploy groups: a node's explicit group wins, then its subgraph's, otherwise the outermost subgraph name, otherwise main.

docs.title: ROS 2 tutorials in Blueprint Studio
docs.text:
The official ROS 2 Humble tutorials teach ROS 2 from the terminal: create a workspace, create a package, write a node, build with colcon, run it. These chapters walk the same path in Blueprint Studio. For every step they show:

  • what you do in Studio instead of the terminal;
  • what Studio generates for you, and where to find it in the project;
  • what still matters: the ROS 2 concepts Studio does not hide, and the places where Studio behaves differently from the official tutorial.

Read the official tutorial alongside: it explains the concepts, these chapters show the tool.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Docker is installed and running (Docker Desktop on Windows). Studio runs ROS 2 Humble in a container, so you do not need a local ROS 2 installation.
  • Studio is installed (see Install). The first Run pulls the ROS 2 image (about 2 GB) and takes a few minutes.

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text: # Studio chapter Official tutorial Status 1 Workspace, package and build Creating a workspace · Creating a package · Using colcon to build packages ready 2 Publisher and subscriber (Python) Writing a simple publisher and subscriber (Python) ready 3 Publisher and subscriber (C++) Writing a simple publisher and subscriber (C++) ready 4 Service and client Writing a simple service and client (C++ / Python) ready 5 Looking at a running system Beginner: CLI tools (nodes, topics, services, parameters, actions, rqt_console, bag) ready 6 Parameters, tuned live Using parameters in a class (C++ / Python) · Understanding parameters ready 7 Launch files Launch: Creating a launch file · Integrating launch files into packages ready 8 Managed (lifecycle) nodes Demos: Managed nodes planned 9 The same project on a real robot (Studio only: Remote tab) planned

docs.title: How the examples were checked
docs.text:
Tip

Every chapter's project was built in Studio and run in a real ROS 2 Humble container; the screenshots and logs come from those runs. If something looks different on your machine, that is a bug: please report it.

docs.title: 1. Workspace, package and build
docs.text: Official tutorials: Creating a workspace · Creating a package · Using colcon to build packages

docs.title: What the official tutorial does
docs.text:
mkdir -p ~/ros2_ws/src && cd ~/ros2_ws/src
ros2 pkg create --build-type ament_python py_pubsub     # or ament_cmake for C++
cd ~/ros2_ws && colcon build
source install/setup.bash

A workspace is a folder with src/; every folder in src/ with a package.xml is a package; colcon build builds them into install/, and source install/setup.bash makes the result visible to ros2 run / ros2 launch.

docs.title: In Studio
docs.text:
One Studio project is one ROS 2 package. Create it in the start window:

  1. Create New Project: type a name. Only lowercase letters, digits and _, starting with a letter: the same rule ROS uses for package names (REP 144). Studio refuses other names instead of producing a package that fails later.
  2. Project Language:
  3. Python (Scripts only): Python nodes, no build step;
  4. C++ (Compilation required): C++ nodes, built with colcon on every Run;
  5. Mixed: both in one package.
  6. Create and Open.

Projects live in Documents/BlueprintStudioProjects/<name> (Show in Explorer opens the folder).

docs.title: What Studio creates
docs.text:
After the first Save (the disk icon in the toolbar; Run saves first as well):

my_project/
├── src/                     <- the ROS 2 package: everything ROS works with
│   ├── python/  or  cpp/    <- one file per node on the canvas
│   ├── launch/              <- generated launch files (chapter 7)
│   ├── CMakeLists.txt       <- C++ projects only, generated
│   ├── package.xml          <- C++ projects only, generated
│   └── config/params.yaml   <- appears when you save parameters (chapter 6)
├── Dockerfile               <- the image the project runs in
├── .blueprint/              <- Studio's own state (canvas, generated-files list); not ROS
└── project_config.json

docs.title: How this maps to the official workspace
docs.text: Official tutorial Studio ~/ros2_ws /root/ros2_ws inside the session container ~/ros2_ws/src/<package> your project's src/, mounted as /root/ros2_ws/src/user_project package name the project folder name ros2 pkg create --build-type ament_cmake a C++ project: CMakeLists.txt and package.xml are generated on Save colcon build done by Run when the project has C++ (colcon build --symlink-install) source install/setup.bash done by Run before starting the nodes

docs.title: Where Studio differs (and what you still need to know)
docs.text:
• Python nodes are scripts, not an ament_python package. The official tutorial adds setup.py, setup.cfg and entry_points so that ros2 run py_pubsub talker works. Studio skips that: the generated launch file starts each Python node as python3 -u <file>. There is nothing to build, so a change to a Python node is live on the next Run. The cost: ros2 run <package> <node> does not work for Studio's Python nodes; use the launch file.
  • CMakeLists.txt is generated, but it is yours too. Studio rewrites it on every Save from the nodes on the canvas and the #includes in your code (it adds find_package and dependencies itself). Put your own additions between # === BLUEPRINT USER BEGIN and # === BLUEPRINT USER END at the end of the file: that block is kept as is.
  • Dependencies are filled from your code. Including nav_msgs/msg/odometry.hpp in a C++ node adds nav_msgs to CMakeLists.txt and package.xml, and ros-humble-nav-msgs to the Dockerfile. Understanding why a package needs a dependency is still on you: it is the first thing to check when a build fails.
  • The container is the workspace. Everything ROS runs inside Docker. Your files stay on your disk; the container only mounts src/. build/, install/ and log/ live in the container.

Important

A local run stays on your computer. Studio starts the session with ROS_LOCALHOST_ONLY=1: your nodes do not see, and cannot command, robots on the same network, even in the same ROS_DOMAIN_ID. Turn on Real robot (toolbar) to open the session to the network; the container is recreated on the next Run when this or the domain/DDS settings change.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. Create a Python project py_pubsub_tutorial.
  2. Press Save: src/ gets python/ and launch/; there are no nodes yet.
  3. Continue with chapter 2.

docs.title: 2. Publisher and subscriber (Python)
docs.text: Official tutorial: Writing a simple publisher and subscriber (Python)

docs.title: What the official tutorial does
docs.text: Two nodes in one package. minimal_publisher creates a publisher on the topic topic and a 0.5 s timer; on every tick it publishes a std_msgs/String "Hello World: N". minimal_subscriber subscribes to the same topic and logs what it hears. They know nothing about each other: ROS connects them because they use the same topic name and message type.

docs.title: In Studio
docs.text:
Start from the Python project of chapter 1.

  1. From the Node Palette drag StringPub and StringSub onto the canvas.
  2. Fill the fields on the nodes:
Node Name Other fields StringPub talker Topic: /chatter, Interval (s): 0.5 StringSub listener (Topic is set by the wire in the next step)

Name is the ROS node name (what ros2 node list shows); the file on disk is named after the node's title on the canvas. 3. Connect out of talker to in of listener. The subscriber takes the publisher's topic: the System Log says 'listener' now uses topic /chatter (wired to 'talker'). 4. Run. Studio saves, starts the session container and launches the nodes.

The output is on the ROS2 Dashboard tab: one row per process with its last message; double-click a row for its whole log.

talker prints Publishing: "Py: 0", listener prints Heard: Py: 0, twice a second. Python nodes appear as python3-1, python3-2: these are launch's process names, numbered in the order of the launch file (talker, then listener here).

docs.title: What Studio generated
docs.text:
src/python/talker.py (comments trimmed), the official publisher with other names:

class talker(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('talker')
        self.pub = self.create_publisher(String, '/chatter', 10)
        self.timer = self.create_timer(0.5, self.timer_callback)
        self.i = 0

    def timer_callback(self):
        msg = String()
        msg.data = f"Py: {self.i}"
        self.pub.publish(msg)
        self.get_logger().info(f'Publishing: "{msg.data}"')
        self.i += 1

src/python/listener.py is the official subscriber: create_subscription(String, '/chatter', self.callback, 10) and a callback that logs Heard: .... src/launch/project_launch.py starts both files.

docs.title: Topics, wires and the Topic field
docs.text:
ROS does not know about the wire. It connects a publisher and a subscriber when their topic names and message types match, and Studio writes the Topic field into the code. The wire keeps the fields in step:

  • connecting a wire gives the subscriber the publisher's topic;
  • changing a publisher's topic changes it on every node wired to it;
  • if wired nodes still end up with different topics (you edited the subscriber's field), Save warns in the System Log: 'talker' and 'listener' are wired but use different topics.

Nodes without a wire talk too, as long as the topics match: that is how ROS works, the wire is for you.

docs.title: Your code stays yours
docs.text: Double-click a node to open its file in your editor. As long as the code is Studio's unchanged template, Studio fills in the names from the node's fields on Save. Once you edit it, your version is kept, and from then on the code decides, not the fields: the ROS node name is whatever super().__init__(...) says, the topic is whatever create_publisher says.

docs.title: Variant: exactly the official publisher
docs.text:
1. Double-click talker and replace the whole file with the tutorial's publisher_member_function.py.
  2. In it, change the topic 'topic' to '/chatter', the one listener subscribes to.
  3. Run. The dashboard shows Publishing: "Hello World: 0" and Heard: Hello World: 0; ros2 node list now shows /minimal_publisher instead of /talker, the name from the code.

docs.title: Check it like the official tutorial
docs.text:
The official tutorial checks the result with ros2 topic echo. The session container is a normal ROS 2 environment, so the same commands work there:

docker exec -it ros2_orchestrator_session bash
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
ros2 node list          # /listener  /talker
ros2 topic list         # /chatter  /parameter_events  /rosout
ros2 topic echo /chatter

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text:
Concept (official tutorial) Where it is in Studio publisher, create_publisher(type, topic, qos) StringPub node, Topic field timer, create_timer(period, callback) StringPub node, Interval field subscriber and callback StringSub node, callback in its file nodes are matched by topic name and type the Topic fields; the wire keeps them equal setup.py entry points, ros2 run not used: the launch file runs the scripts (chapter 1)

Next: the same pair in C++, chapter 3.

docs.title: 3. Publisher and subscriber (C++)
docs.text: Official tutorial: Writing a simple publisher and subscriber (C++)

docs.title: What the official tutorial does
docs.text: The same pair as in chapter 2, in C++: publisher_member_function.cpp publishes "Hello, world! N" every 500 ms, subscriber_member_function.cpp prints what it hears. Unlike Python, C++ has to be compiled, so the tutorial also edits package.xml (dependencies) and CMakeLists.txt (find_package, add_executable, ament_target_dependencies, install), runs colcon build, and starts the nodes with ros2 run cpp_pubsub talker.

docs.title: In Studio
docs.text:
1. Create a C++ project cpp_pubsub_tutorial (chapter 1).
  2. Drag StringPub and StringSub from the palette. On a C++ project the palette offers the C++ versions of the same nodes.
  3. Names talker and listener; Topic /chatter and Interval 0.5 on talker.
  4. Wire out to in: listener takes the topic, as in chapter 2.
  5. Run. Studio saves, generates CMakeLists.txt and package.xml, runs colcon build in the container (the build output goes to the System Log), then launches both nodes.

C++ nodes appear under their executable names (talker-1, listener-2), not as python3-N: the launch file starts them as ROS nodes from the package. It also names each node after its file, the title on the canvas: in a C++ project the Name field is not used (here both are talker and listener, so it does not show).

docs.title: What Studio generated
docs.text:
src/cpp/talker.cpp:

class talker : public rclcpp::Node {
public:
    talker() : Node("talker"), count_(0) {
        publisher_ = this->create_publisher<std_msgs::msg::String>("/chatter", 10);
        timer_ = this->create_wall_timer(std::chrono::duration<double>(0.5), [this](){
            auto msg = std_msgs::msg::String();
            msg.data = "Cpp: " + std::to_string(count_++);
            publisher_->publish(msg);
            RCLCPP_INFO(this->get_logger(), "Publishing: '%s'", msg.data.c_str());
        });
    }
    ...
};

The official code puts the timer callback into a member function bound with std::bind; Studio's template uses a lambda. Both are ordinary rclcpp.

src/CMakeLists.txt, the part the official tutorial writes by hand:

find_package(rclcpp REQUIRED)
find_package(std_msgs REQUIRED)
...
add_executable(talker cpp/talker.cpp)
ament_target_dependencies(talker ... rclcpp ... std_msgs)
install(TARGETS talker DESTINATION lib/${PROJECT_NAME})

and src/package.xml with <depend>rclcpp</depend>, <depend>std_msgs</depend>.

docs.title: How the build steps map
docs.text: Official tutorial Studio add <depend> to package.xml generated from the #includes of your nodes find_package, add_executable, ament_target_dependencies, install generated: one executable per .cpp with main() colcon build --packages-select cpp_pubsub Run builds the whole workspace in the container source install/setup.bash done by Run ros2 run cpp_pubsub talker Run starts the launch file; ros2 run works too (below)

docs.title: Where Studio differs (and what you still need to know)
docs.text:
• Extra dependencies. Every executable is linked with a base set: rclcpp, std_msgs, and also geometry_msgs, sensor_msgs, rclcpp_action, rclcpp_lifecycle. The official tutorial needs only the first two. It builds and runs the same; the build is a little longer.
  • Compile errors are yours to read. Studio runs colcon and shows its output in the System Log. A typo in your .cpp fails the build exactly like in the terminal, with the same compiler message.
  • Helpers without main() are not nodes. A .cpp without int main( is compiled into the nodes that #include its header, and is not started by launch.
  • Your own CMake goes into the USER block at the end of CMakeLists.txt (chapter 1): extra libraries, target_sources, compile options. The rest of the file is rewritten on every Save.

docs.title: Check it like the official tutorial
docs.text:
C++ nodes are a real package, so the official commands work in the session container:

docker exec -it ros2_orchestrator_session bash
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
source /root/ros2_ws/install/setup.bash
ros2 run cpp_pubsub_tutorial talker      # a second publisher, from the terminal
ros2 topic echo /chatter

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text:
Concept (official tutorial) Where it is in Studio rclcpp::Node subclass with a publisher and a wall timer StringPub node (C++), Topic and Interval fields subscription with a callback StringSub node (C++) package.xml dependencies generated from #includes CMakeLists.txt executables and install rules generated; your additions in the USER block colcon build, source, ros2 run Run; ros2 run also works in the container

Next: service and client, chapter 4.

docs.title: 4. Service and client
docs.text: Official tutorials: Writing a simple service and client (Python) · (C++)

docs.title: What the official tutorial does
docs.text:
A topic is a stream: the publisher sends, whoever listens receives. A service is a request and an answer: the client sends a request and waits for the response of exactly one server. The tutorial uses example_interfaces/srv/AddTwoInts:

int64 a
int64 b
---
int64 sum

The server answers with a + b. The client takes a and b from the command line, sends one request and prints Result of add_two_ints: for 2 + 3 = 5.

docs.title: In Studio
docs.text:
The palette has a Services group with two nodes: ServiceServer (orange) and ServiceClient (pink), in Python and in C++.

  1. In a Python (or C++) project drag ServiceServer and ServiceClient onto the canvas.
  2. Fields:
Node Fields ServiceServer Name add_two_ints_server, Service /add_two_ints ServiceClient Name add_two_ints_client, a = 2, b = 3, Interval (s) = 1.0
  1. Connect call of the client to srv of the server. The client takes the server's service name: 'client' now uses service /add_two_ints (wired to 'server'). For services the server owns the name (for topics it is the publisher), because one server answers many clients.
  2. Run.

Every second the client sends a request, the server logs Incoming request: a: 2 b: 3, and the client logs Result of add_two_ints: for 2 + 3 = 5.

docs.title: What Studio generated
docs.text:
The server (src/python/server.py) is the official one:

self.srv = self.create_service(AddTwoInts, '/add_two_ints', self.add_two_ints_callback)

def add_two_ints_callback(self, request, response):
    response.sum = request.a + request.b
    self.get_logger().info('Incoming request: a: %d b: %d' % (request.a, request.b))
    return response

The client (src/python/client.py) differs on purpose:

self.cli = self.create_client(AddTwoInts, '/add_two_ints')
self.timer = self.create_timer(1.0, self.send_request)

def send_request(self):
    if not self.cli.service_is_ready():
        self.get_logger().info('service not available, waiting again...')
        return
    req = AddTwoInts.Request()
    req.a = 2
    req.b = 3
    future = self.cli.call_async(req)
    future.add_done_callback(lambda f: self.get_logger().info(
        'Result of add_two_ints: for %d + %d = %d' % (req.a, req.b, f.result().sum)))

The C++ nodes do the same with create_service / create_client and async_send_request with a callback.

docs.title: Where Studio differs (and why)
docs.text:
• The client asks again and again. The official client is a one-shot program: it reads a and b from sys.argv, calls spin_until_future_complete and exits. A node started by a launch file has no command line and should keep running, so Studio's client sends a request every Interval seconds with the a and b fields. Put a and b in your code instead if you need real input.
  • The answer comes in a callback, never by waiting. call_async plus add_done_callback (C++: async_send_request with a callback). The template does it this way on purpose:

Warning

Never wait for a service response inside a callback (rclpy.spin_until_future_complete in a timer callback, or future.get() in C++). It blocks the node's only executor thread: the response can never be processed and the node hangs. This is the most common service bug in ROS 2. - "service not available" is normal at start. The client may start before the server; it checks service_is_ready() and tries again on the next tick, like the official wait_for_service loop. - Dependencies. example_interfaces is added to package.xml, CMakeLists.txt (C++) and the Dockerfile from the #include / import, as in chapter 1. - C++ node names. In a C++ project the launch file names each node after its file, the title on the canvas (server, client), and the Name field is not used. Python nodes use Name.

docs.title: Check it like the official tutorial
docs.text:
docker exec -it ros2_orchestrator_session bash
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
ros2 service list -t        # /add_two_ints [example_interfaces/srv/AddTwoInts] ...
ros2 service call /add_two_ints example_interfaces/srv/AddTwoInts "{a: 40, b: 2}"

requester: making request: example_interfaces.srv.AddTwoInts_Request(a=40, b=2)

response:
example_interfaces.srv.AddTwoInts_Response(sum=42)

ros2 service call is the terminal's version of the client node: handy to test a server before the client exists.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text:
Concept (official tutorial) Where it is in Studio .srv interface: request --- response example_interfaces/srv/AddTwoInts in the generated code create_service(type, name, callback) ServiceServer node, Service field create_client, call_async / async_send_request ServiceClient node, a, b, Interval client and server are matched by service name and type the Service fields; the wire keeps them equal ros2 service call works in the session container

Next: chapter 5, looking at all of this while it runs.

docs.title: 5. Looking at a running system
docs.text:
Official tutorials: the whole Beginner: CLI tools section: understanding nodes, topics, services, parameters and actions, rqt_console, launching nodes, recording and playing back data.

The official section teaches these tools on turtlesim before you write any code. Here they come after chapters 2 and 4, on your own nodes: a publisher/subscriber pair and a service/client pair in one project. Everything below is real output from that project.

docs.title: Two ways to look
docs.text:
• Studio shows the everyday things without a terminal: logs (ROS2 Dashboard), parameters (Parameters window, chapter 6), node states (Freeze/Unfreeze, chapter 8).
  • The ros2 command line shows everything else. The session container is a normal ROS 2 Humble environment, so every command of the official tutorials works there:
docker exec -it ros2_orchestrator_session bash
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash

This replaces the official Configuring environment step: ROS is installed and sourced in the container, you never install it on your machine. On a robot connected on the Remote tab, the terminal button opens an ssh session there.

docs.title: Nodes
docs.text:
$ ros2 node list
/add_two_ints_client
/add_two_ints_server
/listener
/talker

$ ros2 node info /listener
/listener
  Subscribers:
    /chatter: std_msgs/msg/String
  Publishers:
    /parameter_events: rcl_interfaces/msg/ParameterEvent
    /rosout: rcl_interfaces/msg/Log
  Service Servers:
    /listener/describe_parameters: rcl_interfaces/srv/DescribeParameters
    ...

Every node also has /parameter_events, /rosout and six parameter services: ROS adds them, they are not in your code.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
$ ros2 topic list -t
/chatter [std_msgs/msg/String]
/parameter_events [rcl_interfaces/msg/ParameterEvent]
/rosout [rcl_interfaces/msg/Log]

$ ros2 topic info /chatter
Type: std_msgs/msg/String
Publisher count: 1
Subscription count: 1

$ ros2 topic echo /chatter --once
data: 'Py: 16'
---

$ ros2 topic hz /chatter
average rate: 2.000
    min: 0.499s max: 0.501s std dev: 0.00046s window: 4

$ ros2 interface show std_msgs/msg/String
string data

topic info is the quickest check when a subscriber stays silent: Subscription count: 0 or a different type means the names or types do not match (chapter 2). topic hz confirms the publisher's Interval: 0.5 s, 2 Hz.

docs.text:
$ ros2 service list -t
/add_two_ints [example_interfaces/srv/AddTwoInts]
...

$ ros2 service call /add_two_ints example_interfaces/srv/AddTwoInts "{a: 40, b: 2}"

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
$ ros2 param list /talker
  use_sim_time
$ ros2 param get /talker use_sim_time
Boolean value is: False

ros2 param set works too, but for tuning use Studio's Parameters window (right-click a node → Parameters…): sliders for declared ranges, the node's own refusals shown, values saved into the project. That is chapter 6.

docs.title: Actions
docs.text: ros2 action list prints nothing for this project: none of its nodes has an action. The palette has no action nodes yet; write one in a custom node following the official Writing an action server and client tutorial.

docs.title: Logs: instead of rqt_console
docs.text:
The ROS2 Dashboard tab is Studio's rqt_console: one row per process with its last message, double-click a row for the whole log of that node. The System Log tab is Studio itself: build output, saving, Docker, Remote.

rqt tools need a display. The session image has them, but they need an X server: Studio's X11 (XLaunch) visualization mode (on Windows with XLaunch running). Visualize in the default Foxglove mode needs no X server: topics, plots and 3D in the browser.

docs.title: Recording and playing back data
docs.text:
$ ros2 bag record -o demo_bag /chatter
...
[INFO] [rosbag2_recorder]: Recording...
^C
$ ros2 bag info demo_bag
Files:             demo_bag_0.db3
Duration:          4.499911815s
Messages:          10
Topic information: Topic: /chatter | Type: std_msgs/msg/String | Count: 10 | Serialization Format: cdr

Warning

Stop the recording with Ctrl+C: the bag is closed properly only then. Killing the process leaves a bag without metadata that ros2 bag info cannot read.

ros2 bag play demo_bag                                  # back on /chatter: listener hears it too
ros2 bag play demo_bag --remap /chatter:=/chatter_replay   # or on another topic

The bag is written inside the container. To keep it, write it under the project: ros2 bag record -o /root/ros2_ws/src/user_project/bags/demo /chatter lands in your project's src/bags/ on disk (and is synced to the robot with the rest of src/, so delete what you do not need).

docs.title: 6. Parameters, tuned live
docs.text: Official tutorials: Using parameters in a class (Python) · (C++) · Understanding parameters

docs.title: What the official tutorial does
docs.text: A parameter is a named setting of a node (a gain, a rate, a frame name) that can be read and changed from outside while the node runs. The tutorial declares my_parameter with declare_parameter, reads it in a timer, changes it with ros2 param set, and finally sets it from a launch file so the node starts with the right value.

docs.title: In Studio
docs.text:
Start from the publisher of chapter 2. Double-click talker and replace the whole file with this one: the same publisher, with two parameters, the text it publishes and the period with a declared range.

import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from rcl_interfaces.msg import FloatingPointRange, ParameterDescriptor, SetParametersResult
from std_msgs.msg import String


class Talker(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('talker')
        self.declare_parameter('message', 'Hello world',
                               ParameterDescriptor(description='Text to publish'))
        # a declared range: Studio shows a slider, and ROS refuses values outside it
        self.declare_parameter('period', 0.5, ParameterDescriptor(
            description='Seconds between messages',
            floating_point_range=[FloatingPointRange(from_value=0.1, to_value=2.0, step=0.1)]))
        # called before a new value is accepted: the node can refuse it or react to it
        self.add_on_set_parameters_callback(self.on_parameters)

        self.pub = self.create_publisher(String, '/chatter', 10)
        self.timer = self.create_timer(self.get_parameter('period').value, self.tick)
        self.i = 0

    def on_parameters(self, params):
        for p in params:
            if p.name == 'message' and not p.value.strip():
                return SetParametersResult(successful=False, reason='message must not be empty')
        for p in params:
            if p.name == 'period':              # a new period needs a new timer
                self.timer.cancel()
                self.timer = self.create_timer(p.value, self.tick)
        return SetParametersResult(successful=True)

    def tick(self):
        msg = String()
        msg.data = f"{self.get_parameter('message').value}: {self.i}"
        self.pub.publish(msg)
        self.get_logger().info(f'Publishing: "{msg.data}"')
        self.i += 1


def main():
    rclpy.init()
    node = Talker()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        pass
    node.destroy_node()
    rclpy.shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

Tip

If the node does not show up in the Parameters window, it probably did not start. Double-click its row on the ROS2 Dashboard: a Python traceback there (for example NameError after renaming the class but not the call in main()) tells you why.

Two things go beyond the official example, and both matter on a real robot:

  • The range (FloatingPointRange) is part of the parameter. ROS itself refuses period = 5.0; every tool sees the limits (ros2 param describe prints them); Studio draws a slider over exactly that range.
  • The callback runs before a new value is accepted. Here it refuses an empty message and rebuilds the timer when the period changes. Without it, setting period would change the parameter but not the timer: the official example only reads its parameter in the timer, so it does not need one.

docs.title: Tuning in the Parameters window
docs.text:
Run, then right-click talker → Parameters…

  • period has a slider from 0.1 to 2.0 because the range is declared; message is a text field; use_sim_time is a parameter every node has.
  • Drag the slider: the value is sent while you drag (the latest one, about ten times a second), and the node applies it at once. ros2 topic hz /chatter goes from 2 Hz to 1 Hz when the period goes from 0.5 to 1.0. A ✓ next to a row means the node accepted the value.
  • Type an empty message: the node refuses it. The field goes back to the value the node has, and the node's own reason is shown:

  • Revert sends back the values the node had when the window opened.
  • The Node list picks any running node, not only the one you clicked.

The window talks to the node through a small bridge process in the session container (about 2 ms per change), the same way locally and on a robot connected on the Remote tab.

docs.title: Keeping the values: Save to project
docs.text:
Values set in the window live only as long as the node runs. Save to project writes the ones you changed into src/config/params.yaml, in the standard ROS format:

/talker:
  ros__parameters:
    message: Hi from Studio
    period: 1.0

The generated launch file passes this file to every node (--ros-args --params-file for Python, parameters=[...] for C++), so the next Run starts talker with Hi from Studio every second. This is the official tutorial's last step, change the parameter via a launch file, without editing the launch file. The file is in src/, so it goes to the robot with your code, and you can edit it by hand: Studio merges into it and keeps your own entries.

docs.title: On the real robot
docs.text:
With Real robot on, or with a robot connected on the Remote tab, the window is careful:

  • nothing is sent while you drag; the value goes when you release the slider;
  • a change of more than 20 % of the range in one step, or any change of a number without a declared range, asks for confirmation first;
  • Revert asks too.

Caution

A jump of a gain on a real robot is a jerk of a joint. Declaring ranges in your nodes is what makes these checks possible, and they do not replace the robot's own emergency stop.

docs.title: Check it like the official tutorial
docs.text:
$ ros2 param list /talker
  message
  period
  use_sim_time
$ ros2 param get /talker period
Double value is: 1.0
$ ros2 param set /talker period 5.0
Setting parameter failed: Parameter period out of range Min: 0.1, Max: 2.0, value: 5.0
$ ros2 param set /talker message ''
Setting parameter failed: message must not be empty

The terminal and the window go through the same ROS services, so they see the same values and the same refusals.

docs.title: The same in C++
docs.text:
In a C++ project (chapter 3), double-click talker and replace the whole file src/cpp/talker.cpp with this one. Run builds it with colcon as usual.

#include <chrono>
#include "rclcpp/rclcpp.hpp"
#include "std_msgs/msg/string.hpp"

class Talker : public rclcpp::Node {
public:
    Talker() : Node("talker") {
        rcl_interfaces::msg::ParameterDescriptor period_desc;
        period_desc.description = "Seconds between messages";
        rcl_interfaces::msg::FloatingPointRange range;
        range.from_value = 0.1;
        range.to_value = 2.0;
        range.step = 0.1;
        period_desc.floating_point_range.push_back(range);
        declare_parameter("message", "Hello world");
        declare_parameter("period", 0.5, period_desc);

        on_set_ = add_on_set_parameters_callback(
            [this](const std::vector<rclcpp::Parameter> & params) {
                rcl_interfaces::msg::SetParametersResult result;
                result.successful = true;
                for (const auto & p : params) {
                    if (p.get_name() == "message" && p.as_string().empty()) {
                        result.successful = false;
                        result.reason = "message must not be empty";
                        return result;
                    }
                }
                for (const auto & p : params) {
                    if (p.get_name() == "period") {
                        restart_timer(p.as_double());
                    }
                }
                return result;
            });
        pub_ = create_publisher<std_msgs::msg::String>("/chatter", 10);
        restart_timer(get_parameter("period").as_double());
    }

private:
    void restart_timer(double period) {
        timer_ = create_wall_timer(std::chrono::duration<double>(period), [this]() {
            std_msgs::msg::String msg;
            msg.data = get_parameter("message").as_string() + ": " + std::to_string(count_++);
            pub_->publish(msg);
            RCLCPP_INFO(get_logger(), "Publishing: '%s'", msg.data.c_str());
        });
    }
    rclcpp::Publisher<std_msgs::msg::String>::SharedPtr pub_;
    rclcpp::TimerBase::SharedPtr timer_;
    OnSetParametersCallbackHandle::SharedPtr on_set_;
    size_t count_ = 0;
};

int main(int argc, char ** argv) {
    rclcpp::init(argc, argv);
    rclcpp::spin(std::make_shared<Talker>());
    rclcpp::shutdown();
    return 0;
}
  • Keep the handle on_set_ (an OnSetParametersCallbackHandle::SharedPtr member): when it is destroyed, the callback is removed and the node stops refusing values.
  • In the Parameters window a C++ node also shows qos_overrides.… parameters: rclcpp declares them itself, read-only. Leave them alone.
  • Checked the same way as the Python node: period 1.0 applies, 5.0 is refused by the range, an empty message by the callback.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text:
Concept (official tutorial) Where it is in Studio declare_parameter, get_parameter in your node's code parameter descriptor, range the slider and its limits in the Parameters window ros2 param list / get / set the Parameters window; the commands work in the container refusing a value add_on_set_parameters_callback; the reason shows in the window parameters from a launch file Save to project → src/config/params.yaml → the generated launch

Next: chapter 7, launch files.

docs.title: 7. Launch files
docs.text: Official tutorials: Creating a launch file · Integrating launch files into ROS 2 packages · the rest of the Launch section

docs.title: What the official tutorial does
docs.text: A launch file starts several nodes at once, with their names, namespaces, remappings and parameters, instead of one ros2 run per terminal. The tutorial writes a Python launch file with Node(package=..., executable=..., name=..., namespace=..., remappings=[...]) actions, installs it with the package and starts it with ros2 launch.

docs.title: What Studio does for you
docs.text:
You have been using launch files since chapter 2: Run starts src/launch/project_launch.py, which Studio regenerates on every Save from the nodes on the canvas.

PARAMS_FILE = '/root/ros2_ws/src/user_project/config/params.yaml'

def generate_launch_description():
    ld = LaunchDescription()
    params = [PARAMS_FILE] if os.path.exists(PARAMS_FILE) else []

    # C++ nodes: from the built package
    ld.add_action(Node(package='my_project', executable='talker', name='talker',
                       parameters=params, output='screen', emulate_tty=True))
    # Python nodes: the script itself
    ld.add_action(ExecuteProcess(
        cmd=['python3', '-u', '/root/ros2_ws/src/user_project/python/listener.py']
            + (['--ros-args', '--params-file', PARAMS_FILE] if params else []),
        output='screen', shell=True, emulate_tty=True))
    return ld
  • one action per node on the canvas: Node for C++, ExecuteProcess for Python scripts (chapter 1 explains why Python nodes are scripts);
  • the saved parameters of chapter 6 are passed to every node;
  • for C++ projects CMakeLists.txt installs the launch/ folder with the package, the official Integrating launch files into packages step.

docs.title: Deploy groups: one launch file per group
docs.text:
Select nodes, right-click → Assign to container... and type a group name, say robot for the talker and pc for the listener. On Save you get, next to project_launch.py:

src/launch/robot_launch.py   <- only the nodes of group "robot"
src/launch/pc_launch.py      <- only the nodes of group "pc"
docker-compose.yml           <- one service per group

project_launch.py still starts everything (that is what Run uses). A group file starts its part only: ros2 launch .../robot_launch.py in the session container shows just /talker in ros2 node list. docker-compose.yml runs each group in its own container (built with colcon first when the group has C++), which is how one graph is split between a robot and a PC. The group's container settings (image, DDS, network simulation) are on the Containers tab.

Compose services use host networking and are meant to talk across machines: unlike a local Run, they are not isolated from the network.

docs.title: Your own launch file
docs.text:
Studio rewrites project_launch.py and the group files on every Save, so do not edit them. Everything the generator does not know about (remappings, namespaces, arguments, conditions, event handlers, other packages) goes into your own file in src/launch/. Studio never touches files it did not generate.

src/launch/my_launch.py, which starts Studio's nodes plus a second listener under another name, on another topic:

import os

from launch import LaunchDescription
from launch.actions import ExecuteProcess, IncludeLaunchDescription
from launch.launch_description_sources import PythonLaunchDescriptionSource

HERE = os.path.dirname(os.path.realpath(__file__))
PYTHON = os.path.join(HERE, '..', 'python')


def generate_launch_description():
    return LaunchDescription([
        # everything on the canvas, exactly as Run starts it
        IncludeLaunchDescription(PythonLaunchDescriptionSource(os.path.join(HERE, 'project_launch.py'))),
        # one more listener: same script, another node name, another topic
        ExecuteProcess(
            cmd=['python3', '-u', os.path.join(PYTHON, 'listener.py'),
                 '--ros-args', '-r', '__node:=listener_copy', '-r', '/chatter:=/chatter_copy'],
            output='screen'),
    ])

Start it in the session container:

docker exec -it ros2_orchestrator_session bash
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
ros2 launch /root/ros2_ws/src/user_project/launch/my_launch.py

$ ros2 node list
/listener
/listener_copy
/talker
  • Include, do not copy. IncludeLaunchDescription of project_launch.py keeps your file correct when you add nodes on the canvas.
  • Python nodes take ROS arguments on the command line. The official tutorial renames and remaps with Node(name=..., remappings=...), which needs a package executable. A Studio Python node is a script, so the same goes after --ros-args: -r __node:=new_name, -r __ns:=/robot, -r /from:=/to, -p name:=value. For C++ nodes Node(package=..., executable=...) works as in the official tutorial.

Note

Run does not start your file. Run always starts project_launch.py. Start your own launch file from the container terminal as above (stop Studio's Run first, or you get the nodes twice).

docs.title: Where Studio differs
docs.text: Official tutorial Studio you write the launch file project_launch.py is generated from the canvas on every Save Node(package, executable, name) C++ nodes: the same; Python nodes: ExecuteProcess of the script namespace=, remappings= your own launch file (--ros-args -r for Python nodes) parameters=[...] src/config/params.yaml from the Parameters window (chapter 6) installing launch files with the package done in the generated CMakeLists.txt (C++) one launch file for several machines deploy groups: <group>_launch.py + docker-compose.yml substitutions, event handlers, large projects your own launch file, exactly as in the official tutorials
